Hero Media and Fandom.text: Heroes are the biggest celebrities in Japan. News channels cover rescues live, with helicopters and street cameras racing to every major incident. Ranking shows, talk shows and variety programs fill the schedule with hero interviews, analysis and gossip, and each Hero Billboard Chart JP announcement is a national event. Merchandise is big business: figures, trading cards, posters, costume replicas, snacks and stationery carry heroes' faces and emblems, and All Might goods outsell everything else. Some heroes treat publicity as part of the job. Mount Lady built her name on headline-grabbing captures, Uwabami is as familiar from commercials as from patrols, and Best Jeanist is a fashion icon as well as a top hero. Others avoid cameras entirely, and Endeavor's refusal to play along is a story in itself. Fan culture is everywhere: fan clubs, collector shops, analysis blogs and forums, autograph lines, cosplay, children's lunch boxes. Many young people know heroes' Quirks, special moves and ranking histories by heart, and some keep detailed notebooks. The press shapes careers. A dramatic rescue on camera can make a rookie famous overnight, and a scandal, a careless comment or property damage on video can sink an approval rating within a week. Agencies keep press officers for that reason, and the Hero Public Safety Commission watches public opinion closely.
